targetText: Surplus-value and the value of labour-power vary in opposite directions. A variation in the productiveness of labour, its increase or diminution, causes a variation in the opposite direction in the value of labour-power, and in the same direction in surplus-value.
summary: Inverse variation of surplus-value and wages: productivity gains in wage goods reduce the value of labour-power and raise surplus-value.
explanation: When productivity rises in industries producing food, clothing, and shelter, the value of labour-power falls. Consequently, the capitalist extracts a larger proportion of surplus-value even if the real material standard of living of the worker remains unchanged or rises slightly.
context: Part V, Chapter 17: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labour-Power and in Surplus-Value (Section 1)

targetText: price of labour-power are determined by three circumstances; (1) the length of the working-day, or the extensive magnitude of labour; (2) the normal intensity of labour, its intensive magnitude, whereby a given quantity of labour is expended in a given time; (3) the productiveness of labour, whereby the same quantum of labour yields, in a given time, a greater or less quantum of product, dependent on the degree of development in the conditions of production.
summary: The three determinants of value of labour-power and surplus-value: length of day, labour intensity, and productivity.
explanation: Marx identifies the three fundamental variables governing how value is divided between capital and wages: (1) how long the worker labours, (2) how intensely they work per hour, and (3) technological productivity, which alters the value of basic consumer goods.
context: Part V, Chapter 17: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labour-Power and in Surplus-Value
